title: Gestational diabetes | NHS inform
text:
Gestational diabetes
Gestational diabetes is a form of diabetes that can develop when you’re pregnant. It happens because your body can’t produce enough insulin to regulate your blood sugar (glucose) levels. This means your body won’t be able to deal as well with the extra blood sugar caused by pregnancy.
Gestational diabetes can cause some serious health conditions for you and your baby.
Gestational diabetes normally goes away after you’ve given birth.
Symptoms of gestational diabetes
Most people who have gestational diabetes don’t have any symptoms. You may only find out you have gestational diabetes when your blood sugar levels are tested during pregnancy screening.
You may develop symptoms if your blood sugar levels get too high (
hyperglycaemia
). Symptoms include:
increased
thirst
needing to pee more often than usual
a dry mouth
tiredness
blurred eyesight
genital itching or
thrush
Some of these symptoms are normal during pregnancy. Having one of these symptoms doesn’t necessarily mean you have gestational diabetes.
Speak to your healthcare professional if you’re worried about any of these symptoms.
How will gestational diabetes affect my pregnancy?
Most women who develop gestational diabetes will go on to have normal pregnancies. They’ll also have healthy babies. But gestational diabetes can cause problems.
Your baby may grow larger than usual. This can lead to difficulties during birth. It increases the likelihood of needing induced labour or a Caesarean section.
Gestational diabetes may also lead to you having having too much amniotic fluid (the fluid that surrounds the baby) in the womb (polyhydramnios). This can cause premature labour or problems at birth.
Gestational diabetes can also lead to:
premature birth
pre-eclampsia
your baby developing low blood sugar – this may require hospital treatment
yellowing of your baby’s skin and eyes (jaundice) after birth – this may require hospital treatment
losing your baby (
stillbirth
) – this is rare
You’re also at a higher risk of developing
type 2 diabetes
in the future if you’ve had gestational diabetes.
Causes of gestational diabetes
Your body changes a lot when you’re pregnant.
The hormones you produce when you’re pregnant can make it hard for your body to use insulin. This means you have a higher risk of insulin resistance. This is when your body doesn’t respond properly to the insulin it makes. Some women can’t make enough insulin to overcome this.
Insulin resistance means your body finds it difficult to use sugar properly for energy. It stays in the blood, making your blood sugar levels rise. This leads to gestational diabetes.
Who is at risk of gestational diabetes?
Any woman can develop gestational diabetes during pregnancy. But you’re at a higher risk if:
you’re over 40
your body mass index (BMI) is above 30 – you can use the
NHS website for England BMI calculator
to work out your BMI
you’ve previously had a baby who weighed 4.5kg (10lb) or more at birth
you’ve had gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy
one of your parents or siblings has diabetes
you have a South Asian, Black, African-Caribbean or Middle Eastern family background (even if you were born in the UK)
If any of these apply to you, you’ll be offered screening for gestational diabetes. You may also be offered screening if you’ve had
weight loss surgery
.
How will I know if I have gestational diabetes?
During your first appointment with your midwife or doctor, you’ll be asked some questions. If these show you have 1 or more of the risk factors, you’ll be offered a blood test (HbA1c) to make sure you don’t have diabetes already. You’ll then be offered a screening test for gestational diabetes at 24 weeks.
The screening test is called an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). The test takes about 2 hours.
You’ll be asked to not eat or drink anything for 8 to 10 hours before your OGTT starts. You’ll have a blood test in the morning when you arrive at the clinic.
You’ll then be given a glucose drink, and asked to rest for 2 hours. Then a second blood sample is taken. This will see how your blood is dealing with the glucose.
If you’ve had gestational diabetes in an earlier pregnancy, you will likely be treated for this in your next pregnancy.
Treating gestational diabetes
If you’ve been diagnosed with gestational diabetes, its important to get your blood sugar to a normal level. This can lower your chances of having problems in your pregnancy.
You’ll be given a blood sugar testing kit so you can monitor how well the treatment is working.
Treatments for gestational diabetes all focus on trying to reduce your blood sugar level. They include:
diet
exercise
medication
Diet and exercise
Blood sugar levels may be reduced by
changing your diet
and being more active, if you can. Tell your midwife or doctor before starting an activity you haven’t done before.
You could try gentle exercises like:
swimming
going for a walk
prenatal yoga
If these changes don’t help, you may be prescribed medication.
Read more on diet and exercise on Diabetes UK
Medication
There are 2 medications you could be given to help lower your blood sugar levels.
Metformin
This tablet helps to reduce the amount of sugar produced by the liver. It also makes your insulin work more effectively. It’s taken with, or after, a meal.
Read more about metformin on Diabetes UK
Insulin
Insulin is a hormone that allows sugar to enter the cells and to be used for energy.
Insulin can’t be taken orally because your stomach will digest it. It’s given as an injection using a small needle that goes in just under the skin.
Read more about insulin on Diabetes UK
Monitoring during and after your pregnancy
You’ll be more closely monitored during your pregnancy and birth to check for any potential problems.
You and your baby will also get more monitoring after birth. You’ll be invited to check the diabetes has gone away. This happens at 12 weeks after you have given birth, and then annually. This will again be the HbA1c test.
